name: José Rizal
info: José Rizal (1861-1896) was a Filipino ophthalmologist, writer and reformer of the late Spanish colonial period whose novels Noli Me Tángere and El filibusterismo shaped Filipino nationalism; executed by Spain in 1896, he is popularly considered the national hero.

facts.born: 19 June 1861 in Calamba, Laguna; seventh child of Francisco Rizal Mercado and Teodora Alonso Realonda, leaseholders of land owned by the Dominican Order
facts.died: 30 December 1896 at Bagumbayan, Manila, shot by a firing squad after conviction by a court-martial for rebellion, sedition and conspiracy
facts.role: Ophthalmologist; writer and leading member of the Propaganda Movement in the 1880s; founder of La Liga Filipina, 1892; exile at Dapitan, 1892-1896
facts.known: Noli Me Tángere (1887); El filibusterismo (1891); La Solidaridad; La Liga Filipina; exile in Dapitan; Mi último adiós; execution in 1896

t: Educated at the Ateneo, Santo Tomas, Madrid and Heidelberg, Rizal became the best-known writer of the Filipino Propaganda Movement, which sought reforms for the colony under Spain.
His novels Noli Me Tángere and El filibusterismo, critical of the friars and colonial government, angered the Spanish authorities and are taken together as a national epic.
Though he condemned the Katipunan's uprising, he was tried for rebellion and shot in 1896, and his standing as national hero and his attitude to the revolution remain debated.
dyk: Rizal's farewell poem, now called Mi último adiós, was hidden in an alcohol stove handed to his family after his execution; he had told his sisters in English, "There is something inside it".
ev: José Rizal is born in Calamba, Laguna
He leaves secretly for Spain to study at the Universidad Central de Madrid
Noli Me Tángere is published in Berlin, the year he completes his eye specialisation at Heidelberg
El filibusterismo is published in Ghent
He founds La Liga Filipina in Manila, is arrested and is banished to Dapitan
Arrested at Barcelona after the Philippine Revolution breaks out, he is sent back to Manila for trial
The Rizal Monument by Richard Kissling is inaugurated over his remains in Manila

sections.early:
José Rizal was born on 19 June 1861 in Calamba, Laguna, the seventh child of Francisco Rizal Mercado and Teodora Alonso Realonda y Quintos. The family name was Mercado; Rizal had been added as a second surname under Governor-General Narciso Clavería's decree of 1849 requiring Filipinos to take Spanish surnames. His father's line went back to Lam-co, a Chinese merchant from Fujian who settled in Calamba in 1697, and his mother's included Chinese mestizo, Spanish, Japanese and Tagalog ancestry. His parents leased a hacienda and rice farm from the Dominican Order. His mother taught him the alphabet at three, and the parish priest Leoncio Lopez and his elder brother Paciano, who had lived with Father José Burgos, also shaped him.

He studied first in Biñan and from 1872 at the Ateneo Municipal de Manila, where he graduated as Bachelor in Arts in 1877 with many prizes. In 1872 the Gomburza priests were executed, and in these years his mother was imprisoned for two and a half years on a relative's charge that she had tried to poison him. At the University of Santo Tomas he studied philosophy and letters, then medicine after learning his mother was going blind. In May 1882, with Paciano's secret support, he left for Spain.
sections.rise:
In Madrid Rizal enrolled in medicine and philosophy and letters at the Universidad Central, took lessons in French, German and English, and lived on a tight allowance from Paciano. He joined the Circulo Hispano-Filipino and became a Freemason, a Master Mason in 1884. That year his toast to the painters Juan Luna and Félix Resurrección Hidalgo, saying greatness was not bounded by skin colour or place of birth, made him well known. In 1887 he completed his eye specialisation at Heidelberg under Otto Becker and finished his first novel, Noli Me Tángere, published in Berlin that year.

Back in the Philippines in 1887, he was already labelled a filibustero, a subversive, by the criollo elite. He wrote a petition for the tenants of Calamba against the friars' rent rises; the litigation that followed ended with the Dominicans evicting the tenants and his family, and General Valeriano Weyler had the tenant buildings torn down. Returning to Europe, he annotated Antonio de Morga's Sucesos de las Islas Filipinas, wrote for La Solidaridad under pen names such as Dimasalang and Laong Laan, and in 1890 contested the leadership of the reform movement with Marcelo H. del Pilar, whom most expatriates supported.
sections.deeds:
Rizal's writings for the reform movement called for the Philippines to be made a province of Spain, for representation in the Cortes, Filipino priests in place of Spanish friars, freedom of assembly and speech, and equal rights before the law; he wrote that Filipinos fought "a double-faced Goliath" of corrupt friars and bad government. El filibusterismo, the sequel to the Noli, was published in Ghent in 1891 with borrowed money. Both novels attacked the friars and the power of the Church; his friend Ferdinand Blumentritt, born in Austria-Hungary, wrote that every episode could happen any day in the Philippines. He also wrote essays such as The Philippines a Century Hence and The Indolence of Filipinos, poems and plays, and made about 56 sculptures.

Returning to Manila in 1892, he founded La Liga Filipina, a civic league for moderate reform by legal means, and was arrested on 6 July 1892 and banished to Dapitan in Mindanao. There, in four years of exile, he built a school, a hospital and a water supply, practised medicine, farmed and collected specimens for European museums; a flying lizard, a beetle and a frog were later named rizali after him. He lived in a common-law marriage with Josephine Bracken, an Irish woman from Hong Kong; their son lived only a few hours.
sections.opponents:
The colonial authorities and the friars were Rizal's chief opponents: the authorities rejected the reforms he sought, which Spanish intellectuals such as Morayta, Unamuno and Pi y Margall endorsed, and the Bishop of Cebu refused him a church marriage because he would not return to Catholic practice. The political writer Wenceslao Retana insulted his family in La Epoca, then apologised when challenged to a duel and later wrote his most important biography. On the Filipino side, Andrés Bonifacio denounced him as a coward after he refused to back an armed rising.

His stance on the revolution is disputed. Pío Valenzuela, who consulted him for the Katipunan in 1895, told a Spanish court that Rizal condemned armed struggle, but later said Rizal favoured a rising once Filipinos were well armed, and that he had lied to exculpate him. Miguel de Unamuno called him "the Tagalog Hamlet", a soul that dreaded the revolution while desiring it. Renato Constantino called him a "United States-sponsored hero", promoted by the American colonial government as a peaceful figure over Bonifacio and Apolinario Mabini; Constantino's analysis has itself been criticised for polemicism and inaccuracies.
sections.last:
In 1896, with the Katipunan's rising now a revolution, Rizal left Dapitan on 1 August with Governor-General Ramón Blanco's leave to serve as a doctor to yellow fever victims in Cuba. He was arrested on the way and imprisoned in Barcelona on 6 October, then sent back to Manila for trial. In Fort Santiago he issued a manifesto disavowing the revolution in its present state, saying education and national identity must come before freedom. A court-martial convicted him of rebellion, sedition and conspiracy. Blanco, sympathetic to him, had been replaced by Camilo de Polavieja after pressure from the friars led by Archbishop Bernardino Nozaleda.

On 30 December 1896 he was shot by Filipino soldiers of the Spanish Army, with Spanish troops behind them ready to fire on the executioners if they failed; his last words were reported as "consummatum est". He was buried secretly in Paco Cemetery in an unmarked grave. His sister Narcisa found it and had it marked "RPJ", his initials reversed, and in August 1898 his remains were exhumed. Several historians report that he signed a retraction of his anti-Catholic ideas; others, including Ricardo Pascual and Rafael Palma, judge the document not his or a "pious fraud", and the question remains disputed.
sections.legacy:
The Italian anarchist Michele Angiolillo invoked Rizal's execution when he assassinated the Spanish prime minister Antonio Cánovas del Castillo. La Liga Filipina gave rise to the Katipunan, and Rizal's farewell poem, first printed in Hong Kong in 1897, was quoted in the United States Congress during the debate on the Philippine Organic Act of 1902 and recited by Indonesian soldiers of independence. On 30 December 1912 his remains were placed at Bagumbayan, now Luneta, where Richard Kissling's Rizal Monument was inaugurated a year later. Emilio Aguinaldo had declared 30 December a day of mourning, and the American Philippine Commission made it a day of observance.

No law or proclamation has officially named any Filipino a national hero, but Rizal is popularly held as one. The Rizal Law of 1956 requires schools and colleges to teach his life and works, and the province of Rizal is named after him. Austin Coates and Benedict Anderson believe he gave the revolution a genuinely national character, while Teodoro Agoncillo argued that Bonifacio should be honoured beside him. Rizalista religious movements venerate him, and the Philippine Independent Church canonised him in 1903, revoking it in the 1950s. Monuments stand from Madrid and Heidelberg to Tokyo, Lima and Toronto.

summary: José Rizal, a doctor and writer from Calamba, became the leading voice of Filipino reform under Spain with Noli Me Tángere and El filibusterismo. Exiled to Dapitan in 1892 and shot for rebellion in 1896 although he disavowed the rising, he became the Philippines' best-known national figure, while his views on revolution and his alleged retraction remain disputed.
